DOCUMENT:
Policy Brief: Scaling High-Dose Tutoring in Year 7 Mathematics
Riverside County Education Authority, Policy Unit, January 2026

Summary
In 2024-25 the Authority funded a pilot of high-dose mathematics tutoring for Year 7 pupils in six urban secondary schools. Pupils who received tutoring made substantially more progress than a randomly selected comparison group. This brief recommends extending the programme to all 42 secondary schools in the county from September 2026, at an estimated annual cost of £2.9 million.

The pilot
Tutoring was delivered in groups of three pupils, three one-hour sessions a week, for 30 weeks, during the school day. Tutors were undergraduate and postgraduate students from Riverside University, recruited, trained and paid £16 an hour through the University's Education Department. Pupils were eligible if they had scored below the expected standard in the end-of-primary mathematics assessment.

Of 480 eligible pupils in the six schools, 360 were offered places by lottery, because tutor capacity was limited; the remaining 120 formed the comparison group. Because places were allocated at random, the comparison is a fair one: the two groups had near-identical prior attainment, attendance and demographic profiles at the start of the year.

Results
Progress was measured using the standardised Year 7 mathematics assessment, taken in September 2024 and again in June 2025.

Group | Pupils assessed in June | Mean score, Sept 2024 | Mean score, June 2025 | Gain
Tutored | 342 | 88.0 | 98.6 | 10.6
Comparison | 114 | 87.8 | 93.4 | 5.6

Tutored pupils gained 10.6 points against 5.6 for the comparison group, a gain 89% larger. The difference of five points is equivalent to roughly four months of additional progress, and is in line with the effects reported in the national evidence base for small-group tutoring. Attendance at sessions averaged 87%, and 95% of the pupils offered a place completed the programme.

Teachers in all six schools reported that tutored pupils were more confident in lessons, and four of the six head teachers have asked for the programme to continue.

Proposal
We propose to extend the programme to all eligible Year 7 pupils in the county's 42 secondary schools from September 2026, retaining the design that proved effective: the one-to-one format used in the pilot, three sessions a week for 30 weeks, delivered in school hours by trained university-student tutors. Riverside University has agreed in principle to expand its recruitment, and its Education Department will continue to train and pay tutors.

Around 3,100 pupils a year meet the eligibility criterion across the 42 schools. Of these schools, 26 are in the county's rural districts, between 40 and 75 miles from the University campus; the remaining 16 are in or near Riverside itself, within a short bus ride of the campus, as were all six pilot schools.

Cost
The pilot cost £750 per tutored pupil: £480 in tutor pay (90 hours of tutoring per group, shared among three pupils, at £16 an hour), £220 for university coordination and training, and £50 for materials and assessment. Applying the pilot unit cost to 3,100 pupils gives an annual cost of £2.9 million.

This compares favourably with the Authority's current spending on Year 8 and Year 9 catch-up classes, which cost £1,100 per pupil and have shown no measurable effect on attainment in the last two internal evaluations. We propose that the catch-up budget be wound down over two years and the savings redirected to tutoring.

Risks and mitigations
Tutor quality. All tutors will complete the University's 12-hour training course and be observed twice per term by a school mathematics lead.
Timetabling. Sessions will be scheduled during form time and one weekly mathematics lesson, as in the pilot, so pupils do not miss other subjects.
Evaluation. The Policy Unit will continue to track progress using the standardised assessment and will report to Committee annually.

Recommendation
The pilot provides rigorous, randomised evidence that high-dose tutoring substantially accelerates progress for pupils who start secondary school behind in mathematics. The model is proven and its costs are known. We recommend that the Committee approve £2.9 million a year from September 2026 to extend tutoring to all 42 secondary schools, funded in part by winding down the catch-up class budget.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "Applying the pilot unit cost to 3,100 pupils gives an annual cost of £2.9 million." -- 3,100 pupils x £750 = £2,325,000 (about £2.3 million), not £2.9 million. The headline cost repeated in the summary and recommendation does not follow from the stated unit cost and pupil numbers.
2. [inconsistency] at: "the one-to-one format used in the pilot, three sessions a week for 30 weeks" -- The pilot is described (and costed) as tutoring in groups of three pupils, but the proposal says it will retain 'the one-to-one format used in the pilot'. The delivery format contradicts itself, and the unit cost depends on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Of these schools, 26 are in the county's rural districts, between 40 and 75 miles from the University campus" -- The scale-up assumes the same university-student tutor model and the same unit cost, yet the document states that 26 of 42 schools are 40-75 miles from the University while all pilot schools were a short bus ride away. Tutor travel time/cost and tutor supply for rural schools are never addressed, though the conclusion ('the model is proven and its costs are known') depends on them.

REVIEW:
# Review: Policy Brief on Scaling High-Dose Tutoring in Year 7 Mathematics

The pilot design is good. Allocation by lottery is a real strength, and baseline balance and attrition look fine. But the brief claims the proposal is "the same as what already worked" and that "costs are known". Neither claim survives a close reading of the brief itself. Several problems would change the Committee's decision.

## Critical issues

### 1. The proposal changes the format from groups of three to one-to-one
The pilot section says tutoring was "delivered in groups of three pupils". The Proposal says it will retain "the one-to-one format used in the pilot". These cannot both be true.

- If the one-to-one wording is a slip, it must be corrected, because it is the design the Committee would be approving.
- If it is intended, the scale-up is a different intervention from the one that was tested. It would also triple tutor costs. At 90 hours per pupil and £16 an hour, tutor pay alone becomes £1,440 per pupil instead of £480. That gives a unit cost of about £1,710 and an annual cost of about £5.3 million.

### 2. The headline cost does not follow from the stated unit cost
£750 × 3,100 = **£2.325 million**, not £2.9 million.

£2.9 million implies either about £935 per pupil or about 3,870 pupils. Either the unit cost, the pupil count or the total is wrong, or there are unstated cost lines. The brief says the £2.9 million "follows directly" from the pilot figures, and it does not. The Committee cannot approve a budget whose arithmetic doesn't reconcile.

### 3. Most of the scale-up is in settings the pilot never tested
- All six pilot schools were urban and "within a short bus ride" of the campus.
- 26 of the 42 target schools (62%) are 40–75 miles away.

For student tutors, a one-hour session at a school that far away means a round trip of roughly 2–4 hours. This creates several problems the brief does not address:

- **Cost:** travel time and expenses are not in the £750 unit cost.
- **Tutor supply:** few students will commute this distance three times a week alongside their studies.
- **Delivery:** the 87% attendance figure may not hold.

"Same tutors, same delivery" is not credible for these schools. The brief needs a rural delivery model, such as local tutors, online sessions or block scheduling. That model would need its own costing, and ideally its own test.

### 4. Tutor capacity has not been shown to exist
The pilot was rationed by lottery *because tutor capacity was limited*. The proposed expansion needs much more:

| | Pupils | Groups of 3 | Tutor-hours per week |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pilot | 360 | 120 | about 360 |
| Scale-up | 3,100 | about 1,033 | about 3,100 |

That is roughly 8.6 times the pilot. If the format really is one-to-one, the scale-up needs about 9,300 tutor-hours a week, roughly 26 times the pilot.

"Agreed in principle" is not evidence that the University can recruit, train and supervise this many tutors. All of them would also have to be available in school hours, at fixed times, during the University's own term pattern. The brief should state how many tutors are needed and what the University has actually committed to.

## Significant issues

### 5. The evidence is less complete than presented
- **No uncertainty is reported.** There is no standard deviation, confidence interval or significance test, and no adjustment for clustering by school. With 114 comparison pupils across six schools, the Committee needs to know the margin of error on the 5-point difference.
- **The "four months" conversion is unsupported.** It cannot be checked without the assessment's standard deviation or norms.
- **Outcomes were measured only at the end of the programme.** There is no evidence that the gains persist into Year 8.
- **The qualitative evidence is weak.** Teacher reports of "confidence" are not blind, since teachers knew who was tutored. Also, two of the six head teachers did *not* ask for the programme to continue, and the brief should say why.
- **Completion is reported ambiguously.** "95% completed" equals the share assessed in June (342/360). The brief should report completion, attendance and assessment separately.

### 6. The scale-up leaves no way to evaluate the programme
Every eligible pupil would be tutored, so there would be no comparison group. The proposed "annual tracking" could only show raw gains. The comparison group gained 5.6 points without tutoring, so raw gains will overstate the programme's effect.

This matters more because the rural setting and the delivery model are both untested. A staged rollout or continued randomisation would allow the effect to be measured. Possible approaches include:

- phasing in rural schools one cohort at a time;
- randomising the order in which schools start.

### 7. Tutoring replaces part of the maths timetable
Sessions use "one weekly mathematics lesson". Tutored pupils do not miss *other* subjects, but they do miss some classroom maths. The pilot effect is therefore net of that lost lesson, which is fine. The brief should say so plainly rather than imply that nothing is displaced.

Form time is also typically short. The brief should confirm that three one-hour sessions a week are feasible in schools with different timetables.

### 8. The costing is incomplete
The £750 figure covers only the University's invoices. It leaves out:

- school staff time, such as maths leads observing tutors twice a term, timetabling and providing rooms;
- travel costs for rural schools;
- the cost of the Policy Unit's evaluation;
- possible increases in coordination costs at roughly nine times the scale;
- pay rises needed to recruit tutors in large numbers.

The brief also assumes 100% take-up among the 3,100 eligible pupils. It should state the take-up assumption explicitly.

### 9. The comparison with catch-up classes is not like-for-like
- Catch-up classes serve Year 8 and 9 pupils. Tutoring serves Year 7. Withdrawing catch-up classes removes support from different children, including pupils who were tutored in Year 7 but are still behind.
- "No measurable effect" in internal evaluations is not established at the same standard as the randomised pilot result.
- The size of the savings is not stated, and neither is the source of the rest of the funding ("funded in part").

## Minor points
- The tutor-quality mitigation relies on school maths leads, who will have the least spare time in small rural schools.
- The brief does not say how the six pilot schools were chosen. If they were volunteers or especially well run, the results may not generalise to all 42 schools.

## Overall assessment
The brief has good evidence that small-group tutoring worked in six urban schools near the University. It does not yet support approving £2.9 million a year for all 42 schools. Before the Committee decides, the brief should:

1. Fix the inconsistency between groups of three and one-to-one, and confirm which format is proposed.
2. Correct the cost arithmetic and add travel, school-side and evaluation costs.
3. Set out a costed, feasible delivery plan for the 26 rural schools.
4. Show that the University can supply the required number of tutors.
5. Report the uncertainty around the effect size.
6. Phase the rollout so the effect can still be measured, especially in rural schools.

A reasonable option is to approve expansion to the 16 urban schools now and run a staged trial in the rural schools.
